style_when: the story is regulatory or contractual — a filing, a mandate, a rate notice, a certificate, a purchase order that changed the economics
prompt: Overhead 90-degree flat-lay photograph on a brushed steel control-room desk. Left card is bone-white paper with an unlabelled hand-drawn staircase line in graphite climbing steeply upward; right card is bone-white paper with a flat horizontal graphite line. Between them lies a small brass clock face with no numerals and a blank paper queue ticket stub, one corner of the right card slightly askew. Even diffused daylight from above, muted palette of graphite, bone white, and deep cobalt. 50mm lens, shallow depth of field falling away at edges, fine film grain, no text, no numbers, no logos, split-screen diptych composition with left-right contrast.
negative_prompt: garbled text, random lettering, watermarks, legible numbers, UI elements
rationale: The story is explicitly about two price cards and one decision, so an overhead document still life at a control-room desk grounds the pricing comparison in a real enterprise environment while avoiding the datacenter cliché. Even diffused light and muted paper tones keep the focus on the two line shapes.
subject: two pricing-plan cards showing a staircase cost ladder and a flat fee line
core_thesis: Cloud support is sold either as a share of the monthly bill on a published ladder or as a flat fee, so the buy side's support line crosses a full-time engineer's monthly wage at roughly $190,000 of cloud spend while a flat plan stays at $999.
core_conflict: A percentage-of-spend ladder that escalates with the bill versus a flat fee that buys a queue slot rather than a guaranteed response clock.
composition: top-down split-screen diptych, left card staircase line, right card flat line, slightly off-axis

review.reason: The frame literally stages the article's two pricing mechanisms, a stepped cost ladder versus a flat fee line, so a reader would recognize the support-pricing comparison, though the cards carry no numbers.
